summary: An OS-level agent sandbox (Firecracker microVM, a modified Linux 6.8 overlayfs, and CRIU plus warm-template fork) that checkpoints and rolls back file and process state as deltas. This makes rollback cheap enough for MCTS-style tree search and RL rollout fan-out. It is evaluated by replaying recorded SWE-bench Verified MCTS trajectories against replay, Firecracker-diff, CRIU, and self-hosted E2B baselines.

claims.claim: Checkpoint blocking is about 10.83 ms and restore about 1.86 ms on SWE-bench MCTS trajectories.
claims.evidence: Table 2 weighted average: 10.83 ck / 1.86 rs, versus E2B (diff) 524.4 / 899.7. The arXiv metadata abstract states 14 ms / 5 ms, which does not match the full text read here (the text is likely a different version). Checkpoint time excludes the asynchronous CRIU dump, which is assumed to hide under a 1-9 s LLM inference window.

claims.claim: State-management overhead drops from 23-48% of end-to-end time (E2B diff) to 1-2%.
claims.evidence: Figure 6: 30-iteration Qwen3-Coder-30B trajectory replays across four archetype groups. E2B is invoked through its raw pause/resume primitives. The sample is 24 trajectories (4/4/10/6) each replayed twice; no variance is reported beyond means.

claims.claim: Faster C/R lets agents explore more nodes under a fixed time budget.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from latency only. No experiment measures more nodes explored or a higher SWE-bench resolve rate. The solve-rate motivation in Figure 1 is borrowed from other papers (SWE-Search and others).

claims.claim: RL fan-out keeps GPU occupation at 95-97% versus 77-80% (CubeSandbox) and 29-36% (E2B).
claims.evidence: Figure 7(c) is computed analytically from the measured fan-out time and the T_gen/T_train of Qwen2.5-7B LoRA on 4 GPUs. It is not measured in an actual training run.

patterns.note: Gives concrete evidence that microVM sandboxes can offer millisecond-scale coupled file and process rollback (Table 2).
Process-level C/R lets multiple independently rollbackable agents share one VM (§4.4), an alternative to isolated worktrees; it is not evaluated for parallel coding.
Infrastructure for RL rollout fan-out; no training outcome is reported.
Uses SWE-bench Verified trajectories only as a workload trace, not as a capability benchmark.

methodology.sample: 24 SWE-bench Verified MCTS trajectories (Django, SymPy, Scientific, Tools groups), each replayed twice; 18 trajectories x 5 reps for the fork micro-benchmark.
methodology.baselines: replay+cp, FC-Diff+dm, CRIU+cp, self-hosted E2B (diff), and CubeSandbox for fan-out. These are reasonable and current, though several are authors' prototypes (§6.1).
methodology.models: Qwen3-Coder-30B and MiMo V2.5-Pro trajectories; Qwen2.5-7B for the RL timing.
methodology.variance: Means for most results; p50/p99 only for fork fan-out (Table 3). No CIs.
methodology.ablations: Component latency breakdown and adaptive optimizations (§6.3).

standards.artifacts: No code or artifact URL for DeltaBox in the text, though about 565 lines of C and 1,200 lines of Python are described.

biases.detail: The headline benefit (more nodes explored, implicitly better agents) is never measured. Only C/R latency is.
All workloads are Python SWE-bench repos. JVM processes, with large heaps and JIT state, would stress CRIU and fork-template memory very differently.
Metadata abstract numbers (14 ms / 5 ms) differ from the full-text abstract and Table 2 (10.83 ms / 1.86 ms).
Table 2 and Figure 6 report means over few replays.
Authors benchmark their own system with their own replay harness; baselines are partly their own re-implementations.

coi.affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University IPADS; Ministry of Education Engineering Research Center for Domain-specific OS; Huawei Technologies (3 authors).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: DeltaBox is the authors' own research system. Competitors E2B and CubeSandbox (Tencent) are compared unfavorably. No Huawei product is evaluated.
coi.detail: Huawei co-authorship counts as vendor affiliation. The system is the authors' own, but it is not a commercial product announcement.

verdict_reason: The latency engineering is credible: the per-event table, baselines, and component breakdown hang together. However, the agent-level benefit is asserted rather than measured, evaluation is Python-only trajectory replay, there is no limitations section and no artifact, and the metadata and text numbers disagree. Useful only as sandbox-infrastructure evidence.
applicability: Low for the reference team. A Java ingestion and delivery team running interactive agents in mixed hosts is not doing MCTS or RL fan-out, where millisecond rollback matters. Git worktrees or container snapshots are adequate at human-in-loop cadence. If the team ever runs search-style agents or Best-of-N over Java builds, the main caveat is that CRIU and fork templates of JVM processes (large heaps, Gradle/Maven daemons) are untested here. The paper does not address cross-repo state, spec-driven development, or healthcare constraints.
